title: Tzadi
hook: the letter of tzaddik, the righteous one

segments.voice: Yesterday, peh, the mouth, and Moses slow of speech. Your line was peh is a mouth. Did the kind sentence make it out loud? Today, a letter with a whole person in its name. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

One short phrase in one verse has kept readers arguing. The verse is about Noah. In the King James words: "Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations." Just, here, translates the Hebrew tzaddik, righteous. Fine. But why add in his generations? Was the Torah praising him, saying he stayed good even in a violent age? Or was it quietly holding back, saying he looked good only next to the people around him? The rabbis heard it both ways, and kept both. Today's letter begins the word they were arguing about.
screen: `NOAH: A JUST MAN.` → `IN HIS GENERATIONS.` → `PRAISE, OR A HEDGE?`

segments.voice: Tzadi. The letter makes a ts sound, and it begins tzaddik, a righteous person. Four angles on it. First, the argument. In the Talmud, one sage says: in his generations, and all the more so had he lived among good people, he would have been greater. Another says: in his generations, but not in others. Rashi puts that second view sharply: next to Abraham, he would have counted for little. Rashi brings both readings, side by side, and doesn't pick. Second, what that tells you about the word. A tzaddik in the Torah is not a statue. Noah is called righteous, and a few chapters later he plants a vineyard and gets drunk. The title doesn't mean flawless. It means someone whose life leans toward what's right, inside a real time and place. Third, the family of words. Tzaddik shares its root with tzedek, justice, and tzedakah, the giving Jews owe to people in need. In Jewish law tzedakah is not optional generosity. It's what righteousness looks like with money in its hand. Fourth, the foundation. The book of Proverbs says, in the King James words, "the righteous is an everlasting foundation." Jewish teachers read that as a picture of the tzaddik: someone the world quietly rests on. Not loud, not perfect. Load bearing. So tzadi is a letter with a job description inside it. Righteousness here is not a feeling or a reputation. It's measured in acts, done in your own generation, among the people you actually live with, whether or not anyone better is watching.
screen: `TZADI BEGINS TZADDIK.` · `IN HIS GENERATIONS: TWO READINGS.` · `TZEDEK, TZEDAKAH: JUSTICE IN ACTION.` · `A FOUNDATION THE WORLD RESTS ON.` · then, large: `THE RIGHTEOUS IS AN EVERLASTING FOUNDATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one righteous act. Settle, and breathe. Look around your own generation, your street, your office, your family chat. Where is something a little bit unjust, or a little bit undone? A bill a friend can't cover. A coworker taking blame that isn't theirs. A donation you meant to make. Choose one act you can actually do today, not a feeling about it. Picture yourself doing it, start to finish. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve. The bell holds the time.
Tzadi. The letter that begins tzaddik, the righteous one, and shares its root with tzedek and tzedakah. Today's word.
Your line: tzadi for tzaddik. Today, do the one act you chose, in your own generation, whether or not anyone better is watching. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Jews learn tzadi as the letter of tzaddik, the righteous person, and of tzedakah, the giving to people in need that Jewish law treats as an obligation rather than a choice.

original.note: Hebrew: a righteous person. The word Genesis uses for Noah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tzaddik is a saint who never does wrong.
what it means: someone whose life leans toward justice, in their own time, flaws and all — like Noah.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 6:9 and Sanhedrin 108a's two readings of b'dorotav, carried by Rashi; Proverbs 10:25, tzaddik yesod olam.
